deep.reconstruction:
This is not a derivation. It is one page (folio 21) of a running five-decimal table. The previous page (20) and next page (22) continue it, covering arguments 0.880 to 1.120 in steps of 0.001.

Each row has five entries:
- an argument A;
- a value B;
- the first difference of B (in units of 1e-5, written between rows);
- C = A + B;
- the first difference of C.

Identification (mine, verified numerically): B(A) = log10(1 + 10^(-A)). Hence C = A + B = log10(1 + 10^A). Spot checks:
- A = 1.000: B = log10(1.1) = 0.041393, written 0.04139.
- A = 0.960: 10^(-0.96) = 0.109648, log10(1.109648) = 0.045186, written 0.04519.
- A = 0.980: 0.043249, written 0.04325.
- A = 0.995: 0.041849, written 0.04185.
- A = 1.011: 0.040402, written 0.04040.
- A = 1.025: 0.039178, written 0.03918.
- A = 1.040: 0.037904, written 0.03790.

The table is therefore a table of Gaussian (addition) logarithms. Given log a = A, it lets one find log(1 + a) = C, or log(1 + 1/a) = B, by a single entry. This is used to compute the logarithm of a sum log(m + n) = log m + B(log m − log n) without leaving logarithms.

The C column can also be read inversely: given C = log(1 + a), one recovers A = log a, which handles differences. The C column is printed separately precisely so the table can be entered from either side.

The difference columns give the interpolation steps. Because C = A + B and A advances by exactly 0.001 per row, the two differences always add to 100 units of the fifth decimal (10+90, 9+91, 8+92). This is a built-in arithmetic check.

The left half of the page runs A = 0.960…1.000 (B decreasing 4519→4139). The right half runs A = 1.000…1.040 (B 4139→3790). Differences fall from 10 to 9 to 8 as B' = −10^(−A)/(1 + 10^(−A)) shrinks in magnitude.
errors: None detected. Spot-checked entries agree with log10(1+10^(-A)) correctly rounded to 5 decimals.
All B-differences checked agree with the tabulated B values. In every row the B-difference and C-difference sum to 100, as required by C = A + B.

results.what: Five-place table of B(A)=log10(1+10^-A) and C(A)=A+B=log10(1+10^A), with first differences, for A=0.960..1.040
results.usually_credited_to: Zecchini Leonelli (idea, 1802/03). Gauss published the first practical five-place table in 1812 (Monatliche Correspondenz, 'Tafel zur bequemern Berechnung des Logarithmen der Summe oder Differenz zweier Grössen...'), hence the name 'Gaussian logarithms'.

deep.surprise_reason: This appears to be a manuscript or draft stage of Gauss's well-known 1812 table of addition logarithms, which bear his name. The only detail of mild interest is that the working table existed in his papers around 1809, before publication; nothing mathematically new.

checkable.asserts: C = A + B equals log10(1+10^A) identically (result 0)
